site: Himeji Castle (Himeji-jō, "White Egret Castle"), on Himeyama hill in Himeji, Hyōgo, Japan. Chapter 8, East Asia (ch08_east_asia), slug himeji, vignette id map-monument-ch08-himeji. The atlas position 34.84 N, 134.69 E is correct.
view:
The postcard view from the Sannomaru hiroba, the big lawn just inside Otemon at the south of the castle. The viewer stands near the south end of the lawn and looks north-north-east up at the hilltop.

In frame: the connected keep complex on the skyline. The main keep is right of centre, highest and largest. To its left and lower are the West small keep, with the Inui (north-west) small keep behind it, joined to the main keep by the low Ha corridor-turret (watari-yagura). Every building is white plaster under grey tile. Beneath the complex is one tall stone wall with a concave face, steep at the top and flaring at the foot, topped by a white plaster wall with a grey tile coping. At the foot of the frame is a band of dark pines, with a sliver of lawn or pale gravel.

Cropped out:
- Otemon, which is behind the viewer and is a 1938 rebuild anyway.
- The Nishi-no-maru long corridor at the far left.
- The Hishi-no-mon and the lower gates.
- The East small keep, which is hidden behind the main keep from this side anyway.
- People, lamps, scaffolding and any modern fittings.

Why this view: it is the one every brochure and postcard prints, the white keep standing over its walls. The cluster of small keeps is what tells Himeji apart from a generic single-keep castle. The curved stone wall is the chapter's signature mechanic in arc.md ("the curved batter of the wall face"). The complex is wider than tall, which suits the 92 x 70 landscape frame.

elements.fact: Five roof tiers outside, six floors inside plus one basement (五重六階地下一階). About 31.5 m tall on a stone base of about 14.85 m, about 46 m overall. It is of the lookout type (bōrō-gata): a large hip-and-gable lower block with the upper storeys set on it. Each storey is narrower than the one below. The frame is timber, entirely coated in white lime plaster (白漆喰総塗籠).

The faces carry a mix of triangular gables (irimoya-hafu and chidori-hafu, including a pair set side by side, 比翼) and curved kara-hafu. The arrangement differs from tier to tier and from face to face, so the keep never reads as a stack of identical roofs. Which gable type sits on which tier of the south face was NOT verified in this pass; take it from a photograph.
The top ridge ends in two shachihoko (a fish with a tiger's head), one at each end. They are fired grey tile like the roof, not gold (gold is Nagoya). There is no central spire or finial.

Smoked grey clay tile (hongawara-buki, ibushi-gawara). The tile joints and ridges are sealed with white plaster, so in sun the roofs read silver-grey with fine white lines. That is why the castle looks white from roof to base. The eaves lift only gently at the corners; they are not a Chinese sweep.
Plastered white like the walls (the whole building is 塗籠). The band under each roof is a cool shadow on white, never exposed brown rafters.
Small rectangular lattice windows in rows, read as dark openings in the white walls. There is no external balcony or railing on any storey.

The keep is a connected complex (連立式天守): the main keep, East, West and Inui (north-west) small keeps, and four corridor-turrets (the I, Ro, Ha and Ni watari-yagura) round a courtyard. All eight are National Treasures, designated 1951. Seen from the south, the West small keep stands left of the main keep, joined by the Ha corridor-turret, with the Inui keep behind it further left. The East keep sits north of the main keep, behind it. Each small keep is much lower, with (to my knowledge) three roof tiers; medium confidence on the tier count.

The face is concave, steep near the top and splaying outward at the foot: the 'fan slope' (扇の勾配, ōgi no kōbai), also called sori (反り). The stones are irregular, roughly fitted and wedge-packed (the Ikeda-era walls are mostly uchikomi-hagi). The corners are laid long-and-short alternately (sangi-zumi). The colour is mixed warm grey and grey-brown with dark joints. It is not brick, not smooth ashlar, not a straight slope and not domed.
White plaster with grey tile copings, pierced by loopholes (sama) in circle, triangle and square shapes. At vignette size these are optional dark dots.

The keep stands on Himeyama hill, not at the waterside; the inner moat is far below and behind the viewer on this line. Pines grow on the slopes. The Sannomaru lawn and pale decomposed-granite (masa) gravel paths are in the foreground. The cherry trees in the grounds are real but largely modern plantings, so their omission is a choice, not a correction.

The present keep complex was built by Ikeda Terumasa in 1601–1609. The west bailey (Nishi-no-maru) was added by Honda Tadamasa in 1617–18. An earlier three-storey keep built by Hideyoshi in 1581 was replaced. By tradition the castle was founded by the Akamatsu clan in 1333 or 1346. The standing fabric falls 1 to 9 years past the chapter window of AD 600–1600. This is noted only; the chapter is unchanged. Restorations: the Shōwa dismantle-and-rebuild of the main keep, 1956–64, and the Heisei re-plastering and re-roofing, 2009–15, reopened March 2015. UNESCO World Heritage, 1993.

mustBeRight: The main keep has five main roof tiers; roofs running all the way round count; gable roofs jutting from a tier do not.
The main keep is the tallest and largest building in the picture.
Each storey of the main keep is narrower than the one below it.
The main keep's gables differ from tier to tier; the keep is not a stack of identical roofs like a pagoda.
The main keep shows both triangular gables and at least one curved (kara-hafu) gable.
The top ridge carries two fish ornaments (shachihoko), one at each end; there is no single central spike.
The shachihoko are grey like the roof tiles, not gold.
All building walls are white plaster from the stone to the eaves; no black boarding and no exposed brown timber.
The band under every eave is shadow on white plaster, not brown rafters.
The roofs are grey tile; not green copper, not blue, not black, not orange.
No gold appears anywhere on the buildings.
No storey has an outside balcony or railing.
Windows are small dark rectangles in rows, not large panes or arched openings.
At least one smaller keep stands to the LEFT of the main keep, much lower and with fewer roof tiers, joined to it by a low connecting building.
No smaller keep stands to the right of the main keep at the same depth.
The stone wall under the keeps has a concave face: steeper at the top than at the foot, flaring outward at the base.
The stone wall is irregular fitted stones, not brick courses and not smooth blocks.
The stone wall is lower than the buildings above it; the keep, not the wall, dominates.
The eaves lift only slightly at the corners; there are no sweeping upturned Chinese-style eaves.
No Mount Fuji, no red torii, no people, no text.
deliberatelyWrong: The several walled terraces between the Sannomaru and the keep (the gates, the Bizen-maru and the keep's own base) are compressed into one tall curved stone wall directly under the keep complex. At 92 x 70 the stacked terraces read as noise, and the concave batter is the chapter's signature mechanic, so it is given one clean wall.
Window lattice bars, loopholes, crest tiles, gable pendants (gegyo) and individual tiles are reduced to dark marks and a few white joint lines, or left out. They are below the scale of the vignette.
Otemon (a 1938 rebuild), the Hishi-no-mon, the lower turrets and the Nishi-no-maru long corridor are left out, so the keep complex reads as one shape.
The shachihoko may be drawn up to about twice their true size, so that two read as two at 92 x 70 rather than vanishing into the ridge.
The sky, the pine greens and the cheer are the set's brochure colours, not a real day's. The season is unspecified and cherry blossom is left out on purpose.

lighting:
Bright late-morning sun from the upper right, as the set fixes for every asset. With the view facing north-north-east, that means light from the east-south-east, behind the viewer's right shoulder.

- **The keep:** the south faces are lit. The right-hand side of each projecting gable is brightest, and the left-hand sides and the west faces of the small keeps are in cool shade (plaster mixed with the set's shadow colour, never grey paint).
- **Under the eaves:** under every roof tier runs a band of cool shadow on white. This rhythm of white storey and shadow band is what makes the keep read as tiered.
- **Roofs:** sunlit slopes are silver-grey with fine white joint lines; the eave edges are darker.
- **The stone wall:** the concavity is shown with light. The steep upper part is darker, and the flared foot faces more of the sky and is lighter, so the curve reads as a gradient rather than an outline.
- **Pines:** dark, with sun catching their right-hand edges.

The white has changed over time. The castle is at its whitest since the 2009–15 restoration, when the plaster and the tile-joint plaster were renewed; photographs from before 2009 show it much greyer. Brochure white is right for today.
pitfalls: Painting a pagoda: a symmetrical stack of identical shrinking roofs with a central spire. Himeji is a lookout-type keep with irregular gables that differ tier to tier, and its top ridge has two shachihoko, one at each end.
Gold shachihoko, which belong to Nagoya, or gold trim and green copper roofs, which belong to the Osaka reconstruction.
Black walls or black boarding (Matsumoto, Okayama, Kumamoto). Himeji is white to the eaves, eave undersides included.
Brown exposed rafters under the eaves.
A railed balcony round the top storey (Inuyama and several concrete rebuilds have one; Himeji does not).
Sweeping upturned Chinese eaves. The Japanese corner lift is slight.
A straight trapezoid stone base, as the current code draws it, or a convex, domed one. The face is concave.
Mirror-reversing the complex: from the south the small keeps are on the left. Small keeps on the right is the view from the north.
Putting the East small keep beside the main keep; from the south it is behind it.
Moat water lapping at the keep's foot. The keep is on a hilltop and the moats are far below.
Mount Fuji in the background (Himeji is in Hyōgo, some 400 km away), cherry blossom everywhere, red torii, or Otemon in the foreground as if it were an original gate.
Painting the keep as stone. Only the base is stone; the keep is a plastered timber frame.
Placing gable types tier by tier from memory. The per-tier arrangement on the south face was not verified here, so copy it from a photograph.
gate6: Clear for the exterior vignette: it shows a fortification and palace buildings. One flag for any later level: the top floor of the main keep houses a small shrine to Osakabe (長壁 / 刑部), still maintained with offerings. That makes it a place of active worship inside the building. The vignette does not show it, since it is interior and out of frame. A level that enters the keep's top floor would need a designer ruling first, and arc.md's Himeji row does not mention the shrine yet. The 1945 air raids on Himeji killed civilians in the city, but the castle is not a site of those deaths, and nothing here touches them.
contested: Founding date. Tradition gives an Akamatsu fort in 1333 and a castle by Akamatsu Sadanori in 1346, but both rest on later (Edo-period) chronicles, and some historians treat the Akamatsu founding as unproven. The documented history starts with the Kuroda family and Hideyoshi's three-storey keep of 1581. Keep this as a dispute in the note, not a fact.

Chapter window. What stands is 1601–09 (the keep complex, Ikeda Terumasa) and 1617–18 (the Nishi-no-maru, Honda Tadamasa), just past chapter 8's AD 600–1600. Only the traditional 1346 founding and the lost 1581 keep fall inside it. The note should say so; the chapter is not changed.

Why the stone face curves. The defensive reading (it throws a climber off, like Kumamoto's 'musha-gaeshi') and the structural reading (the concave profile keeps a rubble-backed wall stable) are both given in the literature. The research's phrase 'un-climbable by design' overstates it: such walls were climbable, and the curve makes the top harder, not impossible.

The Meiji sale. The story that the castle was auctioned in the early 1870s for 23 yen 50 sen, and that the buyer abandoned it because demolition cost more, is widely repeated. The buyer, the date and whether the sale was ever completed are disputed.
The 1945 bomb. The story that an incendiary landed on the keep's top floor during the July 1945 raid and failed to go off is repeated, not established.

The whiteness. After the 2015 reopening the keep was called 'too white' (白すぎ). The restorers put this down to fresh plaster, including on the tile joints, that would weather. How white is 'right' depends on the year, not a dispute about the building.

repoCorrections: src/map/monuments.ts, the docstring of 'tiered-roofs': 'five storeys of white plaster under six roofs' has it backwards. It is five roof tiers outside over six floors inside, plus a basement (五重六階地下一階).

src/map/monuments.ts, 'tiered-roofs': the stone base is drawn as a straight trapezoid under the comment 'Straight, not domed.' Both arc.md ('the concave batter', 'the curved batter of the wall face') and content/map/README.md ('curving outward at the foot') call for a concave face. 'Not domed' is right; 'straight' is wrong.
src/map/monuments.ts, 'tiered-roofs': one thin box at x 49.2 stands as a central finial. Himeji's top ridge has two shachihoko, one at each end, and a central spike reads as a pagoda finial.

src/map/monuments.ts, 'tiered-roofs': the drawing is a lone keep, mirror-symmetric, with identical stacked roofs: four walled storeys plus a triangular cap, an ambiguous count of five. The south view has the smaller keeps to the left, joined by a corridor-turret, and the gables vary from tier to tier. Acceptable only as a placeholder silhouette.

content/map/README.md, row 8: correct as far as it goes, but it should name five roof tiers, the two grey shachihoko, and the smaller keeps to the left. 'Eaves turned up at the corners' should be qualified as a gentle lift, not a Chinese sweep.

content/research/arc.md, chapter 8 table: Himeji 'present form 1601–09' lies outside the chapter's AD 600–1600, but carries no flag, whereas Pontcysyllte in chapter 11 is flagged 'just past the chapter window'. Nijō (1603) has the same issue. Also, 1601–09 covers the keep complex only; the Nishi-no-maru is 1617–18.

content/research/arc.md, chapter 8: the Himeji row has no gate-6 note, but the keep's top floor houses a maintained shrine to Osakabe. This matters for any level that goes inside the keep, not for the vignette.
confidence:
Medium. The web verification this task asked for could NOT be done. Every authoritative domain I tried was blocked by the egress proxy: whc.unesco.org, himejicastle.jp, city.himeji.lg.jp, bunka.nii.ac.jp, kunishitei.bunka.go.jp, en/ja/m.wikipedia.org, wikidata, commons, britannica, japan-guide, jcastle.info, archive.org, loc.gov, jstage, ndl.go.jp, Met API and HathiTrust. The session's WebSearch budget was also already spent (200 of 200). Everything above comes from prior knowledge of the sources listed, not from pages fetched in this pass.

- High confidence: five tiers, six floors and a basement; about 31.5 m on a base of about 14.85 m; white plaster over everything, eaves included; grey tile with white joint plaster; grey, not gold, shachihoko, two on the top ridge; the connected complex of one main and three small keeps with four corridor-turrets and eight National Treasures; the dates 1581, 1601–09 and 1617–18; the restorations of 1956–64 and 2009–15; UNESCO 1993; the Osakabe shrine on the top floor; the concave stone-wall profile.
- Medium confidence: from the south, the West and Inui small keeps sit to the left and the East keep is hidden behind; each small keep has three tiers; Otemon is a 1938 rebuild.
- Low confidence: which gable type sits on which tier of the south face. It is deliberately kept out of mustBeRight.

Recommend a re-run with web access, at least against the Himeji City site and a photograph of the south face, before the gables are painted.
